sections.teaching: He is a really nice and approachable professor, and he usually shares his own thoughts and real-life stories in class, which makes the contents very easy to follow and never boring. The lectures are well structured, and he explains abstract ethical concepts using relatable examples, so even if you have no background in the subject, you can still keep up. Before the lesson starts, he takes attendance by QR code, but he never calls on people randomly or puts students on the spot. For those who are shy or afraid to ask questions in class, this professor is honestly your best choice — the atmosphere is relaxed, welcoming, and totally judgement-free.
sections.grading: The grading is very fair and generous. He clearly explains how each component is weighted at the beginning of the semester, and he gives feedback that actually helps you improve. I personally got an A-, and I felt the grade truly reflected how much effort I put in rather than being graded on a harsh curve. As long as you hand in the assignments on time and put in a reasonable amount of work, you don't have to worry about getting a bad grade.
sections.workload: You mainly need to write one essay, do some short quizzes throughout the semester, take part in a simulation game, and finish a group project. None of the assignments are extremely difficult or time-consuming, but they do require consistent effort instead of cramming everything at the last minute. The quizzes are based on the lecture content, and the group project is fairly manageable if you split the work evenly with your teammates. Overall, it is nowhere near the heaviest course, but it's not a zero-effort one either.

sections.content: The course provides a comprehensive overview of fundamental moral philosophies applied to corporate settings, focusing heavily on traditional frameworks like utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and duty-based principles. The reading materials and case studies (such as corporate dilemmas or specific industry examples) offer a solid background for analyzing conflicts of interest. It is highly useful for building general commercial awareness, though it prioritizes broad theory over technical concepts.
sections.teaching: The lectures are highly structured and rely on an interactive case-driven presentation format. The instructor is generally enthusiastic, explaining major abstract legal and philosophical structures through real-world applications. Class discussions and simulation games are a regular part of the weekly routine to keep students engaged with the material.
sections.grading: Evaluation is distributed across integrated tests, individual reflection papers, regular assignments, and class participation metrics. The grading system follows a standard distribution curve, meaning performance margins are highly relative and depend heavily on formatting consistency and addressing specific prompt parameters.
sections.workload: The workload is moderate but requires steady, consistent attention to weekly reading assignments and case write-ups. While the concepts themselves are straightforward and intuitive, keeping up with the group discussions, roleplays, and examination outlines can become slightly demanding towards the end of the term.

sections.content: This course is mainly about ethics, decision making, and how people make choices in real situations. Each class focuses on a different topic. David usually introduces some examples, discusses the pros and cons, and then encourages students to think from a new perspective. The weekly topics are not always clearly separated, but the flow within each class is very smooth. Although it is still an ethics course, I was surprised that it made me think more deeply about my own decisions and values. I would not say it teaches many practical skills, but it is definitely more interesting than a typical ethics class.
sections.teaching: David is a great lecturer and presenter. His classes are engaging and easy to follow. It is clear that he has spent a lot of time thinking about the topics he teaches. What I appreciated most is that he does not simply tell students what is right or wrong. Instead, he encourages reflection and discussion. He feels very genuine and often shares perspectives that make you think about yourself and the world around you. I also felt that I learned something about being a better person from him, even outside the course content.
sections.grading: The grading structure is very spread out. There are two midterm quizzes worth 15% in total. Each quiz has five multiple-choice questions and tests concepts quite deeply. There are eight reading quizzes worth 10%. They are based on the assigned readings and are usually straightforward if you have read the material. Assignments are worth 15% and are graded generously. Case discussions are worth 15%, and participation usually earns full marks. The group project is worth 20%, and the integrated test at the final lecture is worth 25%. Neither of GP and final test grades is released. Overall, I think the grading is quite fair and generous. I did not perform particularly well on the midterm quizzes, and one of my assignments was below average because I missed a question. I was worried about my final grade throughout the semester, but I still ended up with an A range grade.
sections.workload: The workload depends on how seriously you take the readings. Each reading is around 20 to 30 pages, so reading everything carefully can take a lot of time. On the other hand, some students only complete the reading quiz and leave. The course itself is not difficult, but there are many small assessments throughout the semester. Almost every activity carries some marks. None of them are very hard, but you always need to keep the course in mind. Some students may find the constant stream of small tasks slightly annoying.

sections.content:
Module 1: Introducing Business Ethics. In this module, we will briefly introduce the class and
subject matter before we spend four class sessions introducing the three main approaches towards
business ethics (virtue, duty, and consequence) and the importance of putting each of these
approaches in proper context. These four class sessions will each consist of a short lecture and a
longer, hands-on classroom exercise designed to teach how to use these concepts in practical
settings. These topics will be covered in the mid-term examination, which will most likely be
multiple choice or fill-in-the-blanks.
Module 2: Applying Business Ethics. In this module, we will practice the application of business
ethics concepts and frameworks to difficult real-world business situations. We will study five case
studies in which protagonists must make difficult business decisions involving ethics. For each of
these case studies, students will take a stance on which position they will take and support this
stance with logic and evidence

Students will be evaluated on their understanding of the four main approaches to ethical decision-
making and their ability to apply logic and analysis towards making and justifying ethical decisions
without a clear and obvious answer.
- Mid-term. Students will be tested on their knowledge of ethical concepts and approaches, as
well as the business contexts covered using multiple choice, fill-in-the-blanks, and/or short
answer questions. (20% of final grade)
- Debate. Student groups will be evaluated on their usage of logic and evidence to take and
defend a position upon one of the five case studies debated in class. Students will sign up for
a specific case study of interest based on a first come, first served system. Then, the instructor
will randomly assign half of the students signed up for a specific case to one team, and the
other half to the other team. The debate will contribute 25% of the final grade as follows. The
team will be assigned one grade based upon its performance on the debate. The individual
grades will be calculated by multiplying the team’s grade by the percentage of total possible
points that individual received on peer evaluations from other team members. This system
has proven highly effective in deterring free riding. To ensure fairness, the highest and lowest
peer evaluations will be dropped.
- Group research paper. Students will form a team and write a collaborative research paper on a
topic of their choice. Students will be asked to form groups on their own, with those students
who fail to form groups on their own by the deadline being randomly assigned to groups by
the instructor. Each group will select a topic on a business issue of an ethical nature, upon

which different people might reasonably have a difference in opinion. The instructor will
provide three or four pre-approved essay topics that a group might choose; alternatively,
students may propose their own topics for Instructor approval. The essay will be a maximum

The course will consist of eleven two-hour lectures, held once a week. These lectures will be divided
into two modules respectively focused on introducing and applying business ethics.
Module 1: Introducing Business Ethics. In this module, we will briefly introduce the class and
subject matter before we spend four class sessions introducing the three main approaches towards
business ethics (virtue, duty, and consequence) and the importance of putting each of these
approaches in proper context. These four class sessions will each consist of a short lecture and a
longer, hands-on classroom exercise designed to teach how to use these concepts in practical
settings. These topics will be covered in the mid-term examination, which will most likely be
multiple choice or fill-in-the-blanks.
Module 2: Applying Business Ethics. In this module, we will practice the application of business
ethics concepts and frameworks to difficult real-world business situations. We will study five case
studies in which protagonists must make difficult business decisions involving ethics. For each of
these case studies, students will take a stance on which position they will take and support this
stance with logic and evidence.
More specifically, each student will choose one of the five topics and be assigned to one of two six-
or seven-person debate teams focusing on the topic. Sign-ups for topics will occur via Canvas on a
first-come, first-served basis. These two teams will take opposite stances on the topic in question
and debate each other in front of the class. Note that each team will be expected to have researched
both sides of the debate and will be assigned at random to one of the two sides.
The debates will be structured much like the team vs. team parliamentary debates popular among
leading universities in the United Kingdom and the United States. One team will present the case
supporting a pre-specified resolution, while the opposing team will present the case against the
resolution. The format for these team debates will be as follows:
• Opening arguments, positive case (6 minutes): Two members of the positive case team will
present the main arguments why their point of view is correct.
• Opening arguments, negative case (6 minutes): Two members of the negative case team will
present the main arguments why their point of view is correct.
• Rebuttal, negative case (8 minutes): Two other members of the negative case team will rebut
the main arguments made by the positive case team.
• Rebuttal, positive case (8 minutes): Two other members of the positive case team will rebut
the main arguments and rebuttal of the negative case team.
• Closing arguments, negative case (6 minutes): One or two other members of the negative case
team will make closing arguments supporting their point of view.
Closing arguments, positive case (6 minutes): One or two other members of the positive case
team will make closing arguments supporting their point of view.
• Supporting briefs (time not limited): Students who are not members of either case team may
volunteer to make arguments supporting a position to receive participation credit.
The reason that I have adopted a debate format is because you will undoubtedly be challenged to
justify many ethical decisions that you make. Sometimes, others such as bosses, colleagues, or even
prosecutors and/or barristers, will challenge your decision – at other times, you may end up second-
guessing yourself. If you can learn to support and justify your decisions, you will become better not
only at defending your decision afterwards – but also at making the right decision in the first place.
I will wrap up each debate with my own thoughts on the topic.

btw i was so pissed at this class coz genuinely wasted potential ruined by grading i wrote 1881 words in sfq only for it to register like 300 words after i submitted it, now you know even sfq has a word limit, but if JC cant read my shit then someone has to so here you go:
ironic that this course is called business ethics and the individual but it itself is not ethical and not based on the individual.
imo ethics are subjective so i will be as subjective as i can
i understand the course is supposed to be ethics, and the teacher and ta clearly defined the scope of the midterm, but i find the midterm too difficult and occasionally asking questions that were much more in depth to an unnecessary point and relied on occasional guesswork. of course there was a question on mbti because it took up 5 slides of the powerpoint, and of course it is perfectly fine to include a question like that on the midterm because you previously mentioned anything on the slides can be used to test whether we had "in depth understanding" instead of rote memorization, but it is especially ironic when the question asks for the the pairs of opposing letters in an mbti test when the teacher did say that it is not accurate and it is simply a fun way of knowing about people more and moderation is more important and we might want to tailor our behaviour towards others based on the mbti of others, but isnt memorizing the eight letters more counterintuitive to learning about ethics? of course the test is partial credit, and if i didn't spent unnecessary effort memorizing the letters of the mbti i would have lost 2% in an ethics exam. how ironic. and i dont actually know if i got the question correct because turns out protecting intellectual property is probably more important than helping students learn from their mistakes. please at least let us see the questions and what we got wrong.
another question involves actual history that is no where to be seen in powerpoint slides. maybe the teacher wants to reward those who pay attention in class by saying oh aquinas or martin luther was a figure of the 13th and 15th century respectively, etc. but it is especially repulsive when there are questions that ask about a certain time period in history and how the influential figures of that time impacted the philosophy of ethics? absolutely disgusting, and assuming i got that question right, it was only because i watched crash course philosophy and ethics by hank green two days before the exam and vaguely recalled, or guessed, what time period and what figure the teacher is asking about. if this course is about ethics, please ask about ethics. not this history type questions that are quite literally designed to troll students. i seriously dont see the logic behind such questions and although i have heard classmates claim they scored 96% in the incomprehensibly difficult midterm, i respect their effort in going through the course material and having an extremely detailed understanding, even at times doing their own research to learn more about the course content.
another thing to complain about the midterm is the inclusion of some questions related to the e learning content and e research, very related to ethics but since the teacher said it would be on the midterm i have no choice but to spend some extra time to revise this ethics related section of the class.
partial credit also feels a little off putting but i understand it is to deter students from possibly making false claims in real life when they are not sure about it, but with how the midterm paper is set, i feel this just is just designed to play with the students minds.
if there are related courses that i will have to study in the future, i really want an explanation as to why the paper is designed like that, or at least give the answers to the questions because the content we learn is interesting, and i believe we personally benefit from it a lot, but its just really devastating to see such a paper set this way.
next, about the participation. there can be an ethical debate as to whether a student should be awarded participation marks for "pushing the topic forward or contribute to the current topic of ethics" during class, when i initially expected the midterm to be purely about information on the slides. i think it is more ethical to let the teacher quickly finish the content in class and those who hate the class can go home and revise about it and those who are interested can stay behind to engage in further discussions with the teachers, they can talk about it for twenty four hours if they want. but it does make sense to award extra marks to those who can quickly think of relevant information or arguments about the topic in hand because it proves they are paying attention and exhibiting critical thinking. however i do not agree that it should be made as a component that occupies a set percentage of the final grade, it should purely be extra marks that a student can get. to be fair, if everyone were to try to get participation marks by engaging in discussions it would take up a significant portion of lesson time, unless everyone just says one simple line and that would be quick. but a short line wouldnt be able to express what we are thinking about anyways, especially when the teacher will reply with a lengthy opinion.
and then it is about the pop quiz during the debates. i remember the first time it was conducted someone commented that the question is kinda stupid, and the teacher disagreed. i just think the student could have rephrased his opinion and it would make a lot more sense. the first question was asking which country is a victim of scams and the answer is cambodia. now i do agree with the teacher that those who have thoughtfully and attentively read the materials provided should be able to get the answer right. however, based on previous experiences of the lessons where the debate is carried out, there is a lengthy session of students who dont participate in the debate provide their own opinions or arguments that can push the debate forward. this session and the debate takes up most of the time. there were three reading materials, two of which are not strictly related to the debate topic. so when students are tasked to read the materials that is expected to help us understand the debate, they will constantly think about how this is related to the debate, and two of which are not really that related, so i find it reasonable to skip the two because there wasn't anytime left during lessons based on previous experiences to talk about the two. but turns out the pop quiz is about one of the two reading materials. of course the teacher specifically requested us to read them, and hence it is our duty to read them, but by reading material that isn't especially related to the debate, doesn't this just seem like following the teacher's instructions just because he told us to do so?
the second question was even worse, more like asking about geography than actually asking about the students if they read the material. on an ethical debate about a shooting that occurred in san bernardino, asking about whether apple should build a backdoor to the iphones to gain more intel on the shooting, i would expect the question to be at least about ethics, but the question asks which us state is san bernardino in, which is preposterous, especially when the teacher announced later that we wil get partial credit for san bernardino and i think los angeles which are apparently not states. anyone who actually read the questions and followed the instructions without great memory or extraordinary geography knowledge would probably put a random us state like massachusetts or florida or texas something like that, but these will not be awarded partial credits. which i find especially unfair. and to repeat my concern, what does the fact that san bernardino is located in california have to do with the course that talks about ethics? thanks for measuring my ability to understand and apply ethics and its related knowledge through my ability to remember california. and again, how is this supposed to help me understand the debate? this clearly violates the reason my teacher started this pop quiz, which is to help us understand the debate. to understand the debate we have to read the provided reading materials of which some aren't really related anyways like my unc gon get a heart attack if i tell him hes being scammed and cambodia is a country with lots of victim of scams, and san bernardino is in california. wow
the course is called business ethics and the individual but the individual is not really existent. this course is like a taster for freshmen to experience how cruel and painful hkust and society is. we have to immediately find groupmates to team up with, which significantly impacts your grade, especially when the grading of this course is awful. 50% is determined by group work. the group work is graded based on the performance of the whole group, and then multiplied by how other thinks of your contribution. there is already a limited space for an individual to showcase their own knowledge in a purgatory of people bragging about themselves, pulling wild claims out of their asses, or simply a game of connections and socializing. absolute hell for those who lack social skills to quickly sift through the class and identify helpful individuals. of course it is my skill issue that i can't find better teammates, and of course my understanding and application of business ethics is negatively impacted because i can't find better teammates. this course truly explains business ethics through so much group work and its awful grading system. after all businesses are about connections with other people and solving problems to achieve a certain goal. if your partners aren't good, you might as well expect to do terribly in the real business world, which is what can very well be happening within this course. and it is again my skill issue that i am not able to go through and fix the work of my other groupmates because the group is so large and there are so many people and the workload giving you all zeroes. teacher obviously believes in the kindness of classmates, i cannot vouch for that. my abilities are truly dependent on how others think of me, very aligned with what the course teaches about the subjectivity of morality.

sections.content: Honestly, the content of MGMT 2010 under JC was extremely disappointing. The course is supposed to be about business ethics, but instead of teaching anything  insightful, the lectures ended up being long, boring, and packed with random political opinions that had nothing to do with the topic. I get that ethics is supposed to be philosophical, but this one just went all over the place.
sections.teaching: JC’s teaching style was just a disaster. The lectures were painfully boring, often having on without clear structure or takeaway message. He constantly asks students to stand in front of everyone and answer his questions, which might be friendly for extroverts but is completely unfair to introverted students. It creates a stressful classroom atmosphere where people are more worried about being called on than actually learning anything. It looks like a Russian Roulette when he is picking a student to answer his question.
sections.grading:
The grading system was probably the most confusing part of this entire nightmare. Nothing was clearly explained from the start. No one really understood how marks were given or what standards were used. Everything just vague.

The midterm exam is frustrating because no matter how much effort you put in, you’ll likely only end up with a C or B grade. It genuinely seems like there’s no way to get an A in this course unless you somehow magically guess what the professor wants. Honestly, it’s one of those classes where your effort doesn’t seem to matter at all your grade feels ruined from the start. The whole grading process just adds to this sense of chaos and unfairness that defines the course.
sections.workload:
The materials were also overwhelming and not well-connected to what was discussed in lessons. We had to read a ton of case studies and sources every week, but in reality, it neither improved our understanding nor gave us anything applicable to real business situations. I’m honestly not sure how the content was supposed to help us in any future career.

This course easily has the workload of a 30 cred seminar, not a 3 cred course. Every week is packed with mountains of required readings, case studies, and preparation work. You’re expected to read tons of materials before class, most of which are long, and not even discussed properly in lectures. It’s so much reading for so little payoff.

sections.workload:
I would say it's moderate, and John is quite considerate, as he will extend the deadline for the write-up of the essay and postpone the quiz if students request.
For the quizzes, the first one really challenges your memorizing skills, while the second one is very intuitive, and you can score 80+ based on common sense.
For the essay, he encouraged us to use the AI tool, which significantly reduced the workload (such as finding the academic sources from Grok), as long as you are not directly copying the sentences generated from AI, and provide a short reflection paragraph on how you use the AI, you will be fine.
For the group project, you will need to prepare a 5 mins video about an ethical dilemma faced by a business, and write a 3000-word essay with your peers. Noted that you can use the (take-home) midterm essay to further elaborate, as you already wrote around 1500 words in the mt essay, it is not demanding at all for you and your peers write up an extra 1500 words for the group report.

I liked the content alot. Even though I learnt most of it in A level PRS I loved the way the content was taught in a different way and was actually more conclusive than the way it was taught in a levels. It made a lot more sense the way he taught it. For example in A levels we just learnt about Kant and his whole duty ethics and if its your duty thats it you should just follow it. But in his class he applies the social contract theory and explains how social contracts evolved into duties bounded by contracts which evolved into rights. He explained the concepts clearly in one lesson than the way it was taught in a level for months.

The way he taught meta ethics was completely different than a levels as well and I thought it was weird how meta ethics is some applied concept in his class than an study of ethical language but it was a new perspective.

sections.content:
The course will consist of thirteen two-hour lectures, held once a week. These lectures will be
divided into two modules respectively focused on introducing and applying business ethics.
Module 1: Introducing Business Ethics. In this module, we will briefly introduce the class and subject
matter before we spend four class sessions introducing the three main approaches towards business
ethics (virtue, duty, and consequence) and the importance of putting each of these approaches in
proper context. These four class sessions will each consist of a short lecture and a longer, hands-on
classroom exercise designed to teach how to use these concepts in practical settings. These topics
will be covered in the mid-term examination, which will most likely be multiple choice or fill-in-
the-blanks.
Module 2: Applying Business Ethics. In this module, we will practice the application of business ethics
concepts and frameworks to difficult real-world business situations. We will study five case studies
in which protagonists must make difficult business decisions involving ethics. For each of these case
studies, students will take a stance on which position they will take and support this stance with
logic and evidence.
More specifically, each student will choose one of the five topics and be assigned to one of two six-
or seven-person debate teams focusing on the topic. Sign-ups for topics will occur via Canvas on a
first-come, first-served basis. These two teams will take opposite stances on the topic in question
and debate each other in front of the class. Note that each team will be expected to have researched
both sides of the debate and will be assigned at random to one of the two sides.
HKUST MGMT 2010 Fall 2023
3
The debates will be structured much like the team vs. team parliamentary debates popular among
leading universities in the United Kingdom and the United States. One team will present the case
supporting a pre-specified resolution, while the opposing team will present the case against the
resolution. The format for these team debates will be as follows:
• Opening arguments, positive case (6 minutes): Two members of the positive case team will
present the main arguments why their point of view is correct.
• Opening arguments, negative case (6 minutes): Two members of the negative case team will
present the main arguments why their point of view is correct.
• Rebuttal, negative case (6 minutes): Two other members of the negative case team will rebut
the main arguments made by the positive case team.
• Rebuttal, positive case (8 minutes): Two other members of the positive case team will rebut
the main arguments and rebuttal of the negative case team.
• Closing arguments, negative case (6 minutes): One or two other members of the negative case
team will make closing arguments supporting their point of view.
• Closing arguments, positive case (6 minutes): One or two other members of the positive case
team will make closing arguments supporting their point of view.
• Supporting briefs (time not limited): Students who are not members of either case team may
volunteer to make arguments supporting a position to receive participation credit.
The reason that I have adopted a debate format is because you will undoubtedly be challenged to
justify many ethical decisions that you make. Sometimes, others such as bosses, colleagues, or even
prosecutors and/or barristers, will challenge your decision – at other times, you may end up second-
guessing yourself. If you can learn to support and justify your decisions, you will become better not
only at defending your decision afterwards – but also at making the right decision in the first place.

sections.content: The course content was poorly structured and lacked coherence throughout the semester. Topics were introduced without proper context or logical progression, making it difficult to grasp core concepts. Many readings felt outdated or irrelevant, and the lectures failed to connect theory with real-world applications. There was minimal engagement with current ethical issues, despite the course’s stated focus. Assignments didn’t reinforce learning and often felt disconnected from the material covered in class. Overall, the course did not deliver on its promises and left students confused and unprepared. It needs a complete overhaul to meet basic academic standards and student expectations.
sections.teaching: The professor’s teaching was consistently ineffective and frustrating. Lectures lacked clarity and structure, often jumping between topics without logical flow. Explanations were vague, and complex ideas were glossed over or ignored entirely. There was little engagement with students—questions were dismissed, and discussions were rarely encouraged. The professor relied heavily on slides without elaboration, making classes feel monotonous and uninformative. Assignments and exams didn’t align with what was taught, leaving students confused and unprepared. Overall, the teaching failed to foster understanding or interest in the subject, making the course feel like a chore rather than a meaningful learning experience.
sections.grading: The professor’s grading was highly inconsistent and lacked transparency. Criteria were unclear, and similar submissions received drastically different scores without explanation. Feedback was minimal or generic, offering no guidance for improvement. It often felt arbitrary, with grades seeming disconnected from actual performance or effort. Even after seeking clarification, responses were vague and unhelpful. This created confusion and frustration among students, undermining trust in the fairness of the evaluation process. The grading system failed to reflect students’ understanding or progress, making it difficult to learn from mistakes or feel motivated. A more structured and communicative approach is urgently needed.
sections.workload: The workload in this course is excessively demanding and poorly balanced. Weekly assignments, multiple readings, quizzes, and group projects pile up relentlessly, leaving little time to absorb the material or engage meaningfully. Deadlines often overlap, and expectations are unclear, adding to the stress. Even highly organized students struggle to keep up, and the pressure detracts from learning. Instead of deepening understanding, the workload feels like a constant race against time. It’s hard to maintain motivation when the sheer volume of tasks overshadows the course’s educational value. A serious reevaluation of the workload is needed to make it manageable and effective.

sections.content: Not all lectures are useful, but I find the 3 schools of thoughts (virtue, duty, consequentialism), values, stakeholders theory, greenwashing and CSR useful.
sections.teaching: I think it depends on your perspective to decide whether his teaching is good. If you are looking for some hard-core skills, I would say he doesn’t really teach anything that can help you brush up your CV.  However, since it is the 2 credit course, I actually consider him a guest speaker in UST, who are just giving guest lectures, sharing about his stories and some real life examples. At the end of the day, it’s business ethics, don’t expect partial derivatives or price elasticity to be taught. In this way, I’d say Professor Coombes is quite knowledgable and his class is engaging.
sections.grading:
Participation (15%): I don’t know, I’ll assume everybody gets 15 marks cuz it’s just scanning QR codes and answering discussion boards

Quiz 1 (10%): 20/20 (20 MCQs), mean 16
Questions are trivial and short, definitely AI generated, all about memorisation, but the load is light.

Simulation report (25%): 84/100
You have to write an individual report on a group work, which you are in a simulation that you are managing a whole country to deal with a pandemic.
You have to document your experience, decisions you made and the concepts related to the course.
One funny thing happened was that the TA gave me 80 scores originally, which I was so pissed off, so I asked Professor to re-grade it and he gave me 84 marks. In fact, I did the whole thing on my own but a few friends used AI to generate everything and got 85 86 88 marks. So if you feel like your grade is not justified. You can ask Professor to redo the grading.

Presentation video (10%): 91/100, highest, but the lowest is 76 so there’s no margin.
This is the only component graded by the professor, which you will be doing a 5-minute video presentation presenting an ethical dilemma your group faces and solves.
I’d say to ace it, clarity is of utmost importance because the video is short, do not make your scenario too complicated, make sure to explain the background in just 20 to 30 seconds and focus on the dilemma and your solution. Incorporate as much course content as possible.
Also, although you are allowed to do video editing, don’t overdo it as Professor deducts marks on unnecessary complication.

Final project report (15%): score not disclosed, but I think I did well as I put in a lot of effort.
Going further from the video, you will do a deeper, 3000-word analysis on the dilemma you chose and integrate potentially all the course content in it. Theoretically, you will be sharpening your idea as you get feedback on the video, however it is the professor who give you the feedback but it is the TA who grades the report so ummm… good luck, just try your best.
Also, the professor recommends you to put an executive summary that highlights the dilemma and the decision, it will not be counted towards the word count. You can also add an appendix that explains the concept you applied, we also made use of that and resulted in a 4200 word document (while the limit was 2700-3300)

Integrated test (25%): score not disclosed, you have 45 minutes to complete an essay divided into two sub questions. The first part was theoretical, it asks you to elaborate on the ethical dilemma you choose for the project in terms of the 3 schools of thoughts, last year it was values and stakeholders theory. The second part was asking you about adopting a step by step strategy to solve the dilemma.
One funny thing is these are taught before the mid term, so nothing after the mid term was tested, but I tried my best to incorporate concepts taught throughout the whole course, I guess that was what made me stand out.

Overall grade: A+, my groupmates mostly got A range too, good teamwork!!
sections.workload: Workload is very light, the ppt has little substance. Memorising all is doable (unlike Lee Dong Won ISOM 2010 class). Group project also isn’t that tough. Much better than David’s class which you have a lot of reading quizzes and a lot of work to do.

sections.content:
To be frank useless piece of shit, even through this course claims to be “essential” and “necessary” for decision making. At the end of the day, you’d still believe your gut more.

“ Every day, newspaper articles and social media posts blast out a seemingly endless stream of lying,
fraud, and scandalous affairs committed by the rich and the famous. Indeed, you might even think
that these people became rich and famous precisely because they committed such affairs. Given
this, why should you choose to behave ethically in an unethical world? And how should you do it?
This course is intended to help you find your own answers to these questions.
To achieve this goal, we will investigate business ethics – what is right and wrong in conducting
business. Living as individuals, we make ethical decisions every day that affect the quality of our
personal lives. Working in business, we make ethical decisions every day that affect the long-term
success of a business. Much of the time, we are unaware of the consequences of our choices and
make them unconsciously. But our choices sometimes matter more than you might think.
In this course, we will begin by investigating common ways of looking at ethical decision-making,
before applying these approaches towards situations where it’s not clear what choices are ethical or
not. It’s easy enough to moralize and judge – for instance, about a corrupt executive who is stealing
shareholder capital. What if this executive happened to be your younger brother? If he came to you
and privately shared this information – along with his admission that he was under extreme duress
and needed your support – would you report him to be prosecuted and likely jailed? The reality is
that what is right or wrong is never straightforward within the business environment since the
economy is entangled within society. Our goal is to provide you with a foundation for thinking through these extremely stressful situations and making an informed decision that you won’t regret.”

The course focuses on business ethics, but honestly, it’s pretty dull. Most of the material revolves around three schools of ethics, and it feels repetitive. You’ll spend a lot of time discussing the same concepts without much depth.
Overall, while the topics are relevant, the presentations feel repetitive and lack engagement. The focus on theoretical frameworks can make it hard to see their real-world application.
sections.teaching: Teaching-wise, it’s simply boring. Professor John Coombes is a nice guy, but his lectures lack engagement. The content feels like a dry theory class, and many students find themselves zoning out or distracted during his lectures.
sections.grading: The grading is fine if you put in minimal effort. There are participation marks, a group presentation, and an integrated test, but it’s not clear what’s needed for success. The grading criteria are vague, and students often feel confused about what’s expected. However, you can still get a B+ with little effort.
sections.workload: The workload is manageable, with weekly online discussions and a group project. Just showing up and doing the basics can earn you decent grades. Overall, this course feels like a requirement rather than a valuable learning experience.

my score: above average

Debate (25%): Student groups will be assessed on one of the five case studies discussed in class. All the group members were randomly assigned. The team will receive one grade based on its performance in the debate. Individual grades will be calculated by multiplying the team's grade by the percentage of total possible points the individual garnered on anonymous peer evaluations from other team members.Despite receiving positive comments on the debate from the professor, a negative peer evaluation resulted in a deduction from my score, despite actively participating in this group and contributing

Participation: 20% of the final grade.
my score: above average

Quizzes: 10% of the final grade. Achieved full marks.

Not a good idea to give your teammates good peer evaluations because they might not give you back, or some of them don't want others to have a good grade.
There are others' comments who have encountered a situation similar to mine. I believe that the negative peer feedback received is not a result of my free-riding or contributing less than my peers in group projects. However, in this course, teammates are randomly assigned, with group projects accounting for 50% of the overall grade. fucking stupid.
Don't enrol in this professor's class. The grading will traumatize you and ruin your whole semester. it is dehumanized and unfairly rewards those who give poor peer evaluations. Ironically, an unethical grading mechanism is used in an ethics course.

sections.content:
Business ethics:
Normative ethics and meta ethics
Copied from Canvas:
Course Objectives
The course objective is to find ethical values and approaches towards decision-making that fit you
and your personal needs. By spending some time learning different approaches to ethical decision-
making – and spending much more time applying these approaches towards difficult situations –
you will find it easier to make the right decision for you when the time comes. Overall, you will learn to apply ethical theory via critical thinking, enhance your decision-making skills across your
personal and professional lives, and learn more about your own values and those of your peers.
The intended learning outcomes for this course are for you to understand your professional and
ethical responsibility by reaching the following objectives:
• Knowledge: Understand basic concepts and principles of ethical decision-making.
• Skills: Identify ethical dilemmas and apply logical frameworks to reach feasible resolutions.
• Attitude: Appreciate the importance of behaving ethically in society.
This course will additionally emphasize the following objectives, which are not specifically related
to business ethics but constitute crucial training for first-year undergraduates:
• Basic business contexts. Students in this course are expected to be first-year undergraduates
with limited knowledge of the basic reality of business environments. The rich, detailed case
studies used in this course may very well be their first exposure to the business environment.
Course Structure and Content
The course will consist of thirteen two-hour lectures, held once a week. These lectures will be
divided into two modules respectively focused on introducing and applying business ethics.
Module 1: Introducing Business Ethics. In this module, we will briefly introduce the class and subject
matter before we spend four class sessions introducing the three main approaches towards business
ethics (virtue, duty, and consequence) and the importance of putting each of these approaches in
proper context. These four class sessions will each consist of a short lecture and a longer, hands-on
classroom exercise designed to teach how to use these concepts in practical settings. These topics
will be covered in the mid-term examination, which will most likely be multiple choice or fill-in-
the-blanks.
Module 2: Applying Business Ethics. In this module, we will practice the application of business ethics
concepts and frameworks to difficult real-world business situations. We will study five case studies
in which protagonists must make difficult business decisions involving ethics. For each of these case
studies, students will take a stance on which position they will take and support this stance with
logic and evidence.
More specifically, each student will choose one of the five topics and be assigned to one of two six-
or seven-person debate teams focusing on the topic. Sign-ups for topics will occur via Canvas on a
first-come, first-served basis. These two teams will take opposite stances on the topic in question
and debate each other in front of the class. Note that each team will be expected to have researched
both sides of the debate and will be assigned at random to one of the two sides.

sections.content:
It covers the fundamental ethical theories like Deontology, Consequentialism, and Virtue Ethics and explores their history, benefits and drawbacks, practicality, and ultimately their application in the world of business. U will come to realize, however, that ethics is a very subjective topic, where often you will end up justifying certain decisions by cherry-picking ethical theories and arguments.
The course does help you develop an awareness and understanding of the ethical responsibilities of a businessman, as well as how to tackle difficult situations that are inevitable.

sections.content: the content was quite interesting for me, we cover different theories on normative ethics, and go through different case studies and simulations. concepts that are covered include: virtue ethics (eudaimonia), deontology (rights theory), consequentialism (rule-utilitairianism), meta-ethics etc. then there's also the group debate, in which you get to select your topic from a range of different options (but you have to be quick about it since the debating groups fill up fast). lastly, there's a research paper in which you get to select your own topic and then defend it later onwards in the form of a presentation.
sections.teaching: JC is a very friendly and approachable professor, he encourages class discussion and there's bonus points for people on ask/answer questions. he generally tries to get the class engaged, and will often times ask the class questions to make sure they're listening. If you're late to class, just don't bother going in, because he won't take too kindly to that. All said, he's genuinely a great professor who makes this course fun and exciting.
sections.grading: Your grade depends upon your performance in the mid-terms, the group debate, the quality of your research paper, and the oral presentation defending it. Class participation also counts for bonus points. There's also a few mini-quizzes that are held throughout the duration of the group debates. They surround the material of the debate for the day so you have to read the papers on them before going into class. Overall, it shouldn't be too difficult to get a good grade on this course.
sections.workload:
Probably the biggest downside of this course is how heavy the workload is, especially when you consider that it's only two credits. You're expected to go through the different ethical theories, give a mid-term, then prepare for a group debate that is done in teams and usually go for over an hour, this can take up a significant portion of your time, and ofcourse you have to write a 20-page research paper, which is quite demanding if you want it to be of a good standard. lastly, you have to create a short presentation highlighting your paper and then defend it in front of the class.
In conclusion, the workload is quite heavy for a 2 credit course.

sections.grading:
Good grading as he promises to give 25% A-range if possible.
The grade is determined with the below criteria.

1. Participation (20%)
You can earn the participation mark in these ways

-Attendance of a lesson,  in which you MUST attend most of the lesson to participate in class activities

-Raising questions to professors, if you ask a question that JC considers "good", you will get a participation card which increases your participation mark by 1-2

-Writing meaningful comments to a specific debate topic. After midterm, there will be a debate competition for each lesson. You have to write your own thoughts related to the topic in a paper. If JC thinks the comment is impressive, he will give you a participation mark and invite you to share your ideas in front of your schoolmates.  No worries, I did not share my views in the lesson or raise question to JC and still got a good grade.

I don't know the final participation mark as it's not released. However, participation is the most important factor that influences your grade.

2. Midterm (20%)
16% is MCQs, which is a canvas quiz with 25 MC questions.
I got 20/25 (mean 17.65, median 18.29, UQ 19.79, LQ 15.65, Low 10.92, High 23.5)

You have to choose 1-4 correct answers out of 5 options. Yes, 1 to 4 correct option out of 5. if you choose all the correct option, full mark will be given; if you choose part of the option correctly, you get a decimal number score such as 0.25. But, if you get one option wrong even if you have correct options, you get 0 mark in that question. Therefore, if you don't know all the correct answers, better not to guess them.

MCQs are all related to your ability to recite PPTs, in which you have to know all the definitions of concepts, and the data and memorize all the examples.  

4% is essay, which have to be done within 1 hour. I get 4/8 while many people get 6-8/8

Yea so I get 14.8/20 at the end, about mean I think.

3. Pop up quiz (10%)
You will have to do 1 Mc question after midterm every lesson, mc is about the case study, such as where/when it takes place, how it is ended. Again, its a 1-4 out of 5 MC, you don't know how many option is correct.

JC said the result in the first 2 quizzes was satisfactory, so he did not set up the quiz later.

Me:
Quiz 1 1/1 (High 1, UQ 0.63, Median 0.5, LQ 0.5, Low 0)
Quiz 2 0.5/1 (High 1 UQ 0.5, Median 0.5, LQ 0, Low 0)
So I get 7.5/10 at the end

4. Debates (30%) (with 6-7 people a group)
20% is the quality of the debate, I don't know the result but I think I get 18/20. Basically, if you are the first group to do the debate, you get 20/20.
If JC says perfect, you get 20
if JC says excellent, you get 19
if JC says good, you get 18
If JC says okay, you get 17.
Other comment = 16.

10% is peer evaluation, I get 10/10
You have to prepare both side of the debate, so the workload is heavy.

5. Final Group Project,(20%)  an essay related to a business issue.
12% is the quality of essay,
5% is the presentation
3% is bonus mark, which is how interesting is your essay topic.
I get 18/20 at the end

Final Grade: A

sections.content:
n this course, you will learn (1) the ways and reasons for
why people often fail to act in accordance with their own
ethical values, (2) how we can establish what decisions
are “ethical,” (3) how we can promote ethical behavior,
and (4) what the current and future challenges for ethical
behavior are. Importantly, this course will not teach you
what ethical values you should follow. That is up to you
to decide. Rather, the course will help you reason about
ethical values, make informed decisions, and live up to
your own ideals. The guiding principle throughout the
course is that people are not inherently “good” or “bad,”
but that the environment and the incentives they face
affect how ethically they act. This is good news: it is
much easier to change the environment and incentives
than to change human nature! And as members and
future leaders of organizations, this will be your task.

Actually very good content. You learn why people make unethical decisions and the tradeoffs one might face in the business environment. In fact, adults should also learn this course!!!

Course Contents:
Part I. Introduction to Ethics
Week 1, Syllabus & Introduction
Week 2. Introduction to Behavioral Ethics
Week 3. Normative Ethics
Week  4. Moral Ambiguity
Part II. Encouraging Ethical Behaviour
Week 5. Complexity (Quiz 1 on Part I is held)
Week 6. Lying & Deception
Week 7. Caring for Others (Guest Speaker: Effective Altruism with Matthew Chuang)
Week 8. Research (Library Workshop)
Part III. Ethical Challenges
Week 9. Climate Change (Quiz 2 on Part II is held)
Week 10, Artificial Intelligence
Week 11. Policymaking

Week 12. Integrated Test

The assignments are also very fun! Assignment 1 is a negotiation simulation with a random partner, and what you are graded on is the quality of your reflections. Assignment 2 is a policy simulation with your groupmates in your group project. You have to make tough decisions in order to prevent or delay a zombie outbreak from spreading in your fictional country.

The final project is a 10-page negotiation teaching others some specific ethical concept. It is very fun if you have inspiration on what to write (my groupmates watch a lot of dramas, so they have so many thoughts. Me: confusion)
sections.teaching:
David is the nicest professor in HKUST! He teaches very well, has good PPTs, and also replies quickly in emails. Best of all, he provide RVC on Canvas! Additionally you don't need to book appointments with him, you can just walk up to his office and have a chat about life!!!

Furthermore, he proclaimed himself as a master procrastinator, and he understands the mindsets of students that procrastinate. As a result, he gives numerous extensions even for the simplest of reasons, and he rescheduled the integrated test for people who were sick during April/May.

In the integrated test, he gives out free snacks and drinks to everyone!!! Thanks David!!!

sections.grading:
Good grading if you understand the content. Memorising is not required, but you need to have a clear and open mind when doing the final project and integrated test. The integrated test is closed book so the cutoff are more wider.

10% 6 Weekly Reading Quizzes (10%)
10% 2 Short Quizzes 5 MCs each
30% 2 Assignments
25% Group Project
25% Integrated Test

Weekly Quizzes: Very misleading, I got 5/6 even though they were super easy.
Short Quizzes: First is easy (I got 5/5, mean around 3/5), Second is impossible (I got 4/5 fluke, mean around 2/5)
Assignments: Very lenient, I got basically full for both.
Final Project: Looking at previous years, if you make a compelling simulation, it should be above 40/50.

Integrated Test: 2 hours closed book, 35% MCQ/Fill in the blanks, 65% Long questions. I write a lot (too much that David added a warning in the extra pages saying "you should probably stop writing").

As the exam is closed book, the cutoff should be different to previous years (which were online and open book).

I assume that I did good in the project and test. Finally I get A-range.
sections.workload:
For a 2 credit course, the workload is more like 3 credit course. The official contact time is 2 hours per week. But, there is reading material every week which are tested in the reading quizzes or the integrated test.

You also need to arrange times to meet with partner (for assignment 1) or groups (for assignment 2 and final project). Otherwise, the assignments are really easy to complete.

The final project is due during the exam period, so I recommend to start early!!! You have to come up with a full simulation with plot, confidential information, outcomes, and teaching instructions. In 10 pages, my group wrote almost 4000 words!!!

You also cannot 'properly' revise the integrated test as the long questions are always different. In fact, its better to try understand every concept by reading the reading materials and ppt. DO NOT JUST 'MEMORIZE'!

Tip: As David teaches and marks 300 students, it is recommended that your responses are unique and different to your classmates. That way, he will be less bored and may give you better marks (especially in long questions).

sections.content:
This course is divided into 2 modules:

Module 1: Introducing Business Ethics. There are some key concepts you need to revise and remember to use it in the further assessments. Besides, this module will also conclude with an online seminar hosted by HKUST Library on how to conduct research.

Module 2: Applying Business Ethics. In this module, we will practice the application of business ethics concepts and frameworks to difficult real-world business situations. We

sections.teaching:
Prof. Zhang is cute. She has a slightly Mandarin accent, but it is alright, very clear English compared to other Mainland professors in MATH or PHYS courses.

In her class, time for teaching and discussion will be around 50/50. She will introduce some ethics theory first, then there will be some scenarios (both imaginary and real-life events) where you can apply the theories for analysis.

Don't eat or drink or clean up your room or do anything besides attending the class, or she will unleash her anger and your grade will be in hot water. Also, she will cold-call the names who did not turn on the camera or rarely participated in the in-class discussions.

If you get high scores in midterm or final exam, you will get a appreciation message from her. Good.
sections.grading:
Midterm: 20%
Final Exam: 20%
Debate (Performance): 20%
Debate (Peer Evaluation): 20%
Participation: 20%

========================================
Midterm and Final (20% and 20%):

Initially, she said there would be MC questions and fill-in-the-blank questions in midterm. However, there was NONE. The whole midterm was like final, all essay questions, requiring you to analyze different scenarios using ethics theory.

FYI, questions were like "explain whether sb.'s behavior is ethical" (using whatever ethics theories you like), "what would you do?", "what is the ethical issue here?" and "what is the effect of your decision?".

As this is a ethics course, you will get full or near-full mark as long as you show your logics clearly and reasonably. It is easy tbh. If you are coming from HKDSE, write your paragraphs like Liberal Studies. It will help you to score high.

After the midterm, she gave a debriefing session, telling you what answer was considered as a high-quality answer. It helped me a lot. Following her suggestions will secure a good grade.

Eventually everyone gets good scores, extremely high mean as shown at the end.

========================================
Debate (40%):

You are assigned with a case study, and you need to do it like a normal debating competitions. Each students in a group (each group consists of 5-6 students, you can find your own groupmates) are responsible to speak for about 4-5 minutes.

One bizarre thing is that we only got to know the motion and our position TWO DAYS BEFORE the debate, which is much different from debate competitions.

========================================
Participation (20%):

The hardest part.

You need to share your views during discussion time in class. Writing in chatroom is accepted, but the worst part is that participation is not given by attendance, but the quality and quantity of your sharing.

If you want to score high in this section, you need to SPEAK, TWICE OR MORE each lecture.

Bonus marks will be given if you ask questions or share your views on the debates of other groups.

========================================
FYI, this is the score breakdown of this semester:

Midterm: 44/50 (mean 38.03, low 32, high 50)
Final Exam: 49/50 (mean 42.27, low 0, high 50)
Debate (Performance): not disclosed
Debate (Peer Evaluation): 20/20
(remember to cooperate with your teammates)
Participation: not disclosed

Grade: A+
(If you are an introvert like me too, don't give up. There is still hope.)
sections.workload:
Overall speaking, the workload of this course is extremely light. The workload mainly comes from peer pressure.

========================================
Midterm and Final (20% and 20%):

No workload at all. You only need to revise the notes one day before and that's it.

========================================
Debate (40%):

The heaviest workload in this course. You need to prepare a 4-minute scripts, filled with examples and logical deductions, as well as ethics theories.

Our group is assigned for the first debate. And the date arranged was also unfortunate - right during the midterm periods.

My advice: find the best teammate.

========================================
Participation (20%):

If you are taking it in the spring semester, that means you are in Pathway 2. And essentially, it means fierce competitions. Your classmates are students from GBUS, DDP, ECOF, MAEC, QFIN, RMBI and etc.

Everyone was just competing to speak and share during the class. Often you will see a whole page of students who are holding their hands and waiting to be called to speak. If you are shy like me, try not to be shy. Or else even the Grade God from Goop could help nothing.

sections.content:
Basically, the syllabus structure is about teaching + applying.
At first, he would teach us the following normative and meta-ethics:
- Normative Ethics: Virtue Theories
- Normative Ethics: Duty Theories
- Normative Ethics: Consequentialism
- Meta-ethics & the Cultural Context
As well as a library research methods lecture, covering some very useful research platforms that can be directly accessed through the hkust library portal. And the PPT used during the research lecture would be given later so we can go back and check any time.

Then we would have a chance to practice the ethical theories later in the course in the form of group debating. We get to choose the topic early in the semester and the case materials are given for our reference. However, you could choose your groupmates as everybody had the access to the topic excel sheet, in which we typed our names under the topic.
*For this semester, I found a pattern that students in the same topic will be separated into two teams by the order that the names were typed.
i.e. first 7 names typed were in one group and the rest 7 names were in another group.

Then there were 2 mid-terms. Mid-term 1 is a closed-book MC exam including 25 MCQs and we had 60 mins to complete. And those questions can have multiple answers (Yes, you heard it right, MCs in MCs)
Mid-term 2 is a take-home essay, an argumentative essay with max. 1500 words. The essay structure is actually similar to the Opening part of the debate.
sections.teaching:
JC is really good at teaching. To be honest, the content itself is not really interesting but JC makes it enjoyable to attend the lectures. When explaining those ethical concepts, he would give some real-life examples that students can relate to. You can easily understand what he is talking about as he does not speak in monotone.

What makes his ethical lesson special is that he does teach us how to apply it in lifelike settings, so you can use them flexibly.

We are given some ethical questions to discuss during the class most of the time. It does help us in understanding the concept as JC would push us to think further. However, it left just adequate time for JC to explain the concepts. Thus, you may need to study some theories in-depth outside of the classroom.
sections.grading:
Grading Structure:
Mid-term 1: 15%
Mid-term 2: 25%
Debate: 30%
Participation: 20%
Pop Quizzes: 10%

The participation points are not given based on attendance but how many times you contribute to the class discussions. Here are a few ways to earn points: raise your hands and speak when JC asks a discussion question, write your comments/thoughts about the debate topic/ content debated after a debate is finished.
Participation Cards are given out and you may earn 1 or 2 points for each contribution.

Mid-term 1 itself is not so difficult but the grading mechanism is. Other than MCs in MCs, you cannot go back to the previous questions after you click NEXT. So be careful guys. For each question, only correct options are given partial marks i.e. you need to choose all correct options to earn the entire 1 mark, otherwise, you just get marks in decimal numbers. And here is the trouble part, you will lose the entire mark if you choose a wrong option (no matter how many correct options you chose).

For the debate, you'll be assigned in a group of 6-7 (depending on class size). And you get to decide which role you gonna take within the group (Three roles: Opening, Rebuttal, and Closing). The schedule can be quite tight depending on which topic you choose, for example, Topic 1 Team debate first.
Some tips for getting higher marks in Debate.
- The first team may receive bonus points for debating first (as said to be a linear grading for Debate)
- Outstanding performance may bonus points. Not only winning the debate but also need to give a high-quality debate

It was said that there might be up to 5 pop quizzes for the case materials but ended up 2 quizzes were given. The quizzes were quite easy, just make sure you read the case material carefully and in detail. They are closed-book quizzes (given out in Canvas) and JC really has close eyes on that.

I eventually got an A, and feel I deserve it!!! I really put my effort and time into the course, especially the Debate.
sections.workload:
The workload can be heavy. The debate could really take a chunk of time especially if there is a free-rider in the group :)
The preparation for pop quizzes and raising questions for debates can be time-consuming as well. Because it requires you to read through several case materials.

sections.teaching:
Mark, the lecturer, is very interactive. He encourages every student to participate in the in-class discussion. He is funny and can explain the content quite well. He encourages students to express different ideas and gives responses.

Barry, the tutor, is very helpful. He tells us how to do our group presentation well and reminds us of the details and rubrics of it. He is also very responsible as he keeps reminding us and makes sure everyone submits the work in time and joins the tutorials.
sections.grading:
It is given that the top 20% of students will get A range, the bottom 20% of students will get C range, and the remaining 60% of students are in B range. Most of the students get B range, quite good grade in general.

Components:
30% weekly canvas discussion
35% group presentation
35% final test

The score you get from the above components determines your range of grade. The subgrade will be given based on your activeness of class participation. If you answer the questions actively, you will get A+/B+/C+, vice versa.

I finally get a B+. I did not spend too much time and effort on this course and I think my works are just average. I joined the online discussion every week. I answered a few questions throughout the course, not too much, but most students do not ever answer one question. It is enough to just answer once every lecture and I think the instructors can recognise you and give you a + grade.

Reminder: you have to participate in every lecture and assigned tutorial, attendance is taken. Every absence will result in a 2% deduction in your total score.
sections.workload:
You have to post an online discussion on canvas every week and read an article every week for the next lecture. It is not hard at all but it is quite boring as you have to do it every single week.

The group presentation is a topic about business ethics (you suggest it) It is a 7-10 mins presentation. It is not heavy for individuals as you will have 5-7 persons in a group.

The final test was held in the last lecture. You will write an essay about the topics discussed in the lectures. You can bring the notes along with you. Not difficult if you do not sleep in class.

For classes, there is one lecture every week and two tutorials throughout the semester.

The workload is not too heavy but it is only a 2-credit course. It does not worth too much time for you to study this course.

sections.content: This course presents and exemplifies three major traditions of ethical thought in East and West moral philosophy - namely utilitarianism, principle-based ethics and virtue-based ethics. Employing guest speakers, lectures, cases, contemporary readings, role-plays, fieldwork, reflective student writing, and discussion groups, the course engages students in a serious consideration of their own ethical standards as applied to their present academic environment and their future careers. Students come to understand through this course that while an ethical dilemma may be viewed in various ways depending on one's guiding assumptions, a decision and course of action nevertheless must be chosen in harmony with one's own moral convictions. For Business students only.

sections.grading:
10% Participation
20% Pop Quiz
20% Group Project (Debate)
10% Peer Evaluation
20% Mid-term 1
20% Mid-term 2

For Participation, you have to attend the lessons and most importantly, give contribution during the lesson. Every time, when a group finishes the debate, we as audience could comment about it. This is the chance to get participation credit.

For the Quiz, the Professor actually messes up a bit with the system, so it is casually distributed to the students. It involves the reading of the given materials. There is a tight time limit but if you use the search function wisely, very easy to find the answer. No need memorization.

This debate is essentially a group project. If you win in the debate, you should receive slight more marks. All the groups have their marks varied between 16-19, so even if you lost the debate you got okish mark. As usual, getting a freerider and my debate score goes below mean.

Mid-term 1 requires you to answer 7 short questions in given time. The timing is tight and the questions are quite difficult, very theoretical.

Mid-term 2 is an essay that gives you 3 days to complete it. There are 3 topics to give some flexibility.
sections.workload:
As you can see in the grading section, the workload is large.

First, you have to attend the lessons. In my case, it is a morning 2 hours lecture. To attain more participation mark, you have to unmute and speak something that has quality.

Second, there are pop quizzes. You have to spend time reading the case studies given and not miss the lesson.

Third, you have Mid-term 1. Even though there are not much content in this Course, you have to study to get a high mark in this exam.

Fourth, you have this debate project. Note that this project requires you to do both positive and negative side. Provided that your group has no freeriders and 6 people in total, each people have to do at least one section, sometimes the powerpoint. You also bear the pressure of getting low mark in peer evaluation. Yeah, I do not like these 2 systems.

Lastly, you have Mid-term 2. You have to spend 3 days trying to figure out your arguments and give evidence etc. to do the essay.

Overall, its workload is large.

I just spoke in some of the lessons, I only shared the news once and I did not post a lot on the online discussion board but it is still alright. For the group project, follow his guidance and marking scheme. The key is to show why the topic is controversial and your group's position. And for the integrated task, include some concepts he taught during lessons and in the ppt/assigned readings then it would be fine. It is not necessary to write many words. At last, I got an A grade.

If you have any questions about how the professor grade on something, just email the TA and he would answer you friendly. The grading is not transparent. But if you send an email to the professor in hope of appeal your grade, the TA may tell you your scores for each part (from my frd's experience)

Btw, remember not to miss any lessons.

The content is BORING and you mostly learn how to bullshit your views when you're given an ethical dilemma.

Content: ( = Topic,  = Reading)
 Ethical theories
      Utilitarianism, Duty-based ethics, Virtue ethics
 Resolving dilemmas

 Voicing out

 False advertising

 CSR

 Code of ethics

 Bribing

 Whistleblowing

This course doesn't teach anything concrete or useful. Around 60-70% of lesson time is reserved for "bullshitting time" when everyone can discuss the pros and cons of some business ethics topics (eg. "Should whistleblowers get paid?"). The professor didn't do much wrap-ups or reflections after each discussion ends and I feel like these discussions exist for the sake of existing. Personally, I didn't benefit much from those discussions.

The course also didn't really teach much ethical theories and most of the theories are taught at the first 2~3 weeks.   This may be good if you hate learning boring theories 🤣
sections.teaching:
Professor
I'd say his teaching is okay since he is enthusiastic and very interactive with the students. He encourages discussion in the class by asking everyone to share their thoughts on ethical controversies. His English is also very fluent since he is a Canadian.

However, if you are an introverted student who never speaks in class like me, you would find the lesson very boring. It feels like the things they're discussing is unimportant.

 TA
The TA is friendly and nice. You only need to attend 2 tutorial sessions and meet the TA for 15 minutes. Your group need to report your project progress to the TA in the second tutorial. Even though our group hadn't even started doing anything when we met the TA, he was perfectly fine with that xD
sections.grading:
The grading is extremely NON-TRANSPARENT since they didn't release ANY of your marks and it's also subjective. I got a B+ and I have no fucking idea why I got this grade 🤷‍♂️🤷‍♂️🤷‍♂️

Grading Scheme (ONLINE Semester)
 Online discussion board - 30%
 Group presentation - 35%
 Integrated test (essay writing) - 35%
 -2% of final score for every SKIPPED lesson/tutorial

 Online Discussion Board (30%)
There are 3 discussion topics for each week and you need to submit at least one posting for EVERY WEEK. They didn't tell how your postings will be graded too. Time to practice your bullshitting skills here.

 Group Presentation (35%)
You'll be randomly assigned to teams of 6 and come up with a business ethics controversy to present for 10 minutes. The team need to come up with a topic with the format similar to online discussion topics (eg. "Should companies use false advertising?"). Then, discuss this controversy in both pro and con sides, then finally make a group position.

 Integrated Test (30%)
The test is done at the final lesson where you have 2 hours write an essay. There are 2 prompts to choose from and you need to make reference to TWO assigned readings. They are open-ended questions that asks you to discuss ways to combat unethical behaviors in workplace.

 Attendance Policy
Your final grade will be DEDUCTED for 2% for EVERY SKIPPED LESSON / TUTORIAL!! The professor is scummy enough to hide this information in the middle of the course syllabus document  I saw that there were at least 10 people not attending in every lesson...

Class Participation (25%):
Because of the COVID-19, class participation is completely different from the previous semester. You can choose either answer questions through in class or just fill in the online form after class. Attendance is also counted. I attend all the lecture and fill in all the online forms, but never raise hands and speak in class, but still get a good grade! Presentation on an issue within a specific industry in Asia (at least two countries/regions)

Personal Reflection Essay (15%):
Reflection on the lecture topic. Remember to use some references you read, use your personal experiences (the most important element) as examples and show your maturity.

sections.teaching: The in-class teaching is quite good. The topics are not boring and they are all worthwhile to take a look at. Mark encourages discussion in the class. However the guidance on how to complete the course work is extremely unclear. There is very limited guidance on how to complete the project. sections.grading: The grading is really subjective and unpredictable. You can't even have a correct expectation towards your grade until it strikes you. There is no grades released for the weekly posting, the integrated test nor the presentation. What's so disastrous about the weekly posting is that there is no clear instruction of when-when is counted as "a week". So some people assume that it will be sun-sat while the others would assume that is mon-sun. The problem of having a wrong assumption is that you will miss some weeks if you do not post on the exact some day every week. Another thing is class participation. Every 2% will be deducted for every lesson missed. However, in this term, we don't have iPRS as classes are conducted online. Therefore you won't know if late would be counted as absence, and how many minutes should be considered as "late" as well. For the integrated test, the instruction is super unclear that you won't even know what to write for it. There is no marking for the integrated test either so you wouldn't know how you performed. The same happens to group project. There is no grade for the project nor the presentation. Overall speaking, the transparency of this course grading is extremely poor. I got a C+ and I had no idea what had happened.
sections.workload: If you aim for a good grade, the workload can be heavy. Otherwise, the workload is just mild and you can expect to get a C. First of all class participation is required. Otherwise 2% will be deducted for each class missed and that is disastrous. Also, there is weekly discussion. If you miss it, your grade will be heavily affected as well. You will need to study the reading materials before every lecture so that you can complete the weekly posting and the integrated test, which can actually be quite demanding. The workload for the group project isn't really heavy and I would say it's easy to handle. For this semester, we can decide on the business controversy ourselves and we only need to dig into the pros and cons, the stakeholders and our stance supported by several examples over the world.
